reconcile.note: Gill argues Chronicles' 'Timna' is not a distinct son but a shorthand notice of the same woman Genesis names as Eliphaz's concubine and Amalek's mother.

discrepancy.note: Wellhausen treats the Chronicler's 1 Chronicles genealogical lists as a later, artificial genealogical system reshaping earlier names, of which this Timna entry is one instance.

quotes.text: The penchant for pedigrees and genealogical registers, made up from a mixture of genealogico-historical and ethnologico-statistical elements, is a characteristic feature of Judaism … the inclination to give a genealogical expression to all connections and associations of human society whatsoever, to create artificial families on all hands
quotes.attr: Julius Wellhausen (d. 1918), Prolegomena to the History of Israel (1885), on the artificial, later character of the Chronicler's genealogical registers in 1 Chronicles.

sides.snippet: Timna was concubine to Eliphaz, Esau's son; and she bore to Eliphaz Amalek.
sides.verseText: Timna was concubine to Eliphaz, Esau's son; and she bore to Eliphaz Amalek. These are the sons of Adah, Esau's wife.

sides.snippet: The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, and Omar, Zephi, and Gatam, Kenaz, and Timna, and Amalek.
sides.verseText: The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, and Omar, Zephi, and Gatam, Kenaz, and Timna, and Amalek.
